Mastering: Strengths of geocentric model — matched observations (with epicycles), philosophically consistent with Aristotle, explained why Earth did not appear to move or why no stellar parallax was detected with the naked eye [2 marks for two developed strengths]. Limitations of geocentric — required increasingly complex epicycles, could not explain the phases of Venus, predicted positions becoming less accurate as data improved [2 marks for two developed limitations]. Heliocentric model advantage — simpler explanation of retrograde motion (line-of-sight effect as planets orbit the Sun), naturally explains Venus phases, correct prediction of relative orbital radii [2 marks for developed comparison]. Total 6 marks.
Secure: Four points present, one or two underdeveloped.
Developing: Two or three points, limited development.
Emerging: One point; no comparison made.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following wavebands can be observed from the ground at sea level?
A) X-rays
B) Gamma rays
C) Radio waves
D) Extreme ultraviolet
practice_questions.marks: C [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State two advantages of CCDs over photographic film for recording astronomical images.
practice_questions.marks:
One mark each (up to 2) for any of:
• Much higher quantum efficiency (detect ~90% of photons vs a few % for film) [1]
• Data stored as digital files that can be processed, stacked and analysed on computers [1]
• Linear response (brightness proportional to detected photons) [1]
• Reusable; no need to replace film after each exposure [1]

practice_questions.text: Explain why a single radio telescope dish needs to be much larger than an optical telescope to achieve a similar angular resolution.
practice_questions.marks: Angular resolution depends on wavelength divided by aperture diameter [1]. Radio wavelengths (centimetres to metres) are millions of times longer than optical wavelengths (hundreds of nanometres) [1]. Therefore, to achieve the same resolving power as an optical telescope of a given size, a radio dish must be far larger — or multiple dishes must be combined using aperture synthesis to simulate a larger aperture [1].

practice_questions.text: Compare the advantages and limitations of ground-based optical telescopes and space-based telescopes for astronomical observation.
practice_questions.marks:
Ground-based optical:
• Advantage: much cheaper to build and maintain; can be upgraded; large mirrors achievable (e.g. 10 m class telescopes) [1]
• Limitation: atmospheric absorption blocks non-optical wavebands; atmospheric seeing blurs images even in visible light [1]

Space-based:
• Advantage: no atmospheric absorption — can observe all wavebands; no atmospheric seeing — achieves diffraction-limited resolution [1]
• Limitation: expensive to build and launch; cannot be easily repaired (though HST was serviced by shuttle missions); mirror size limited by launch vehicle fairing [1]

Mark up to 4: 1 per correct paired comparison point, max 2 per telescope type.

practice_questions.text:
Megan Cartwright is a student at the Holt Astronomy Group who wants to observe a newly discovered young stellar object (a protostar) hidden inside a dense molecular cloud. She asks whether she should use an optical telescope, a radio telescope or an infrared space telescope.

Evaluate which type of telescope would be most suitable for this observation and explain why the other two options are less effective.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5-6): Recommends infrared space telescope (e.g. JWST); explains that the molecular cloud absorbs visible light so the protostar is invisible to optical telescopes (dust is opaque to visible); infrared radiation penetrates dust clouds because infrared wavelengths are longer and less scattered; space-based removes atmospheric water-vapour absorption that blocks mid-infrared from the ground; radio telescopes would detect cold molecular gas surrounding the region but not the thermal emission of the protostar itself; optical telescope would see only the dark cloud silhouette or surrounding stars, not the hidden protostar.

Secure (3-4): Recommends infrared; explains why visible light is blocked by dust; some explanation of why radio and optical are less effective; may omit space vs ground distinction.

Developing (1-2): Recommends a plausible telescope with limited justification.

Emerging (0): Irrelevant or no response.

practice_questions.text: The Very Large Array (VLA) uses 27 dishes spread across a maximum baseline of 36 km. Explain what aperture synthesis is and why this technique is necessary for achieving useful resolution with radio telescopes.
practice_questions.marks: Aperture synthesis links multiple smaller dishes electronically to simulate the resolution of a single dish equal in size to the maximum separation (baseline) between them [1]. This is necessary because single dishes of 36 km diameter are impractical to build [1]. Radio wavelengths are so long that even a 36-km effective aperture achieves only moderate angular resolution compared with optical telescopes [1].

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following correctly states Kepler's First Law of planetary motion?
A) The orbital periods of planets are proportional to their distances from the Sun
B) Planets sweep equal areas in equal times as they orbit the Sun
C) Each planet orbits the Sun in an ellipse with the Sun at one focus
D) The gravitational force between the Sun and a planet obeys an inverse square law
practice_questions.marks: C) Each planet orbits the Sun in an ellipse with the Sun at one focus [1 mark].

practice_questions.text: State what is meant by 'perihelion' in the context of a planet's orbit.
practice_questions.marks: The point in a planet's orbit at which it is closest to the Sun [1 mark].

practice_questions.text: Saturn has an orbital period of 29.46 years. Use Kepler's Third Law to calculate Saturn's mean orbital radius in astronomical units. Give your answer to three significant figures.
practice_questions.marks: State Kepler's Third Law: T² = r³ (in years and AU) [1 mark]. Substitute: r³ = 29.46² = 868 (to 3 s.f.) [1 mark for correct substitution]. Take cube root: r = ³√868 = 9.54 AU [1 mark for correct operation]. State answer with units: Saturn's mean orbital radius is 9.54 AU [1 mark]. (If student uses T² / r³ = 1 as their starting equation, this is equivalent — accept.)

practice_questions.text: Explain what contribution Tycho Brahe made to the development of the heliocentric model, and why his work was essential for Kepler.
practice_questions.marks: Brahe compiled the most accurate naked-eye observations of planetary positions over two decades [1 mark], achieving precision of about one arcminute [1 mark]. Kepler needed data accurate enough to distinguish between circular and elliptical orbits; without Brahe's precision records, the small deviations from circularity (e.g. the discrepancy of 8 arcminutes in Mars's position) that forced Kepler to adopt ellipses would not have been detectable [1 mark].

practice_questions.text: Marcus Oyelaran and his astronomy group in Cardiff are investigating how Newton's law of universal gravitation explains stable planetary orbits. Describe how gravitational force produces a stable circular orbit, and explain what would happen if the orbital speed were too low.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Gravity acts as the centripetal force [1] directed toward the Sun, keeping the planet on its curved path [1]. At the correct orbital speed for a given radius, the gravitational force exactly provides the required centripetal force [1]. If the orbital speed is too low, gravity exceeds the centripetal force needed and the planet spirals inward or falls toward the Sun [1]. Newton's inverse square law means that gravity decreases with the square of distance [1], so at a larger orbital radius, less centripetal force is needed and planets orbit more slowly — consistent with Kepler's Third Law [1].
Secure: Four or five points present.
Developing: Correct description of centripetal force and gravity, but incomplete on consequences of wrong speed.
Emerging: States gravity keeps planets in orbit but no further development.

practice_questions.text: Compare Kepler's contribution to the development of the heliocentric model with that of Copernicus, giving two differences.
practice_questions.marks: Difference 1: Copernicus retained perfectly circular orbits; Kepler showed from Brahe's data that orbits are ellipses [1 mark each side = 2 marks]. Difference 2: Copernicus's model was conceptual (placed the Sun at the centre) but not more accurate in predictions than Ptolemy's; Kepler's laws gave precise mathematical predictions that matched observation significantly better [1 mark each side = 2 marks].

practice_questions.text:
What is the Chandrasekhar limit?
A) The maximum temperature at which a star can fuse hydrogen
B) The maximum mass a white dwarf can have and remain stable (1.4 solar masses)
C) The minimum mass required for a protostar to begin nuclear fusion
D) The maximum distance at which a parallax angle can be measured
practice_questions.marks: B [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State what is meant by hydrostatic equilibrium in a main-sequence star.
practice_questions.marks: The balance between outward radiation pressure produced by nuclear fusion in the core [1] and inward gravitational force pulling the star's material inwards [1].

practice_questions.text: Explain why a high-mass star evolves much faster than a Sun-like star.
practice_questions.marks: High-mass stars are far more luminous than Sun-like stars [1]. To maintain this greater luminosity they fuse hydrogen at a much faster rate [1]. Even though they contain more hydrogen, they exhaust it far more rapidly, spending far fewer years on the main sequence compared with a Sun-like star [1].

practice_questions.text: Compare the end stages of a star of 1 solar mass and a star of 20 solar masses. Include the final remnants and the forces that support them (or fail to).
practice_questions.marks:
1 solar mass star:
• Ends as a white dwarf after shedding a planetary nebula [1]
• Supported by electron degeneracy pressure up to the Chandrasekhar limit [1]

20 solar mass star:
• Ends in a Type II supernova; core remnant becomes a neutron star (or black hole if core mass exceeds ~3 solar masses) [1]
• Neutron star supported by neutron degeneracy pressure; above ~3 solar masses no force can halt collapse — black hole forms [1]

practice_questions.text: The following objects are listed in the NGC catalogue: NGC 1952 (the Crab Nebula, a supernova remnant), NGC 7293 (the Helix Nebula, a planetary nebula) and NGC 4486 (M87, an elliptical galaxy with a supermassive black hole). For each object, state what type of stellar end-product it represents or contains and explain what observation or measurement provides evidence for the nature of the central remnant in each case.
practice_questions.marks:
NGC 1952 (Crab Nebula): remnant of a massive star supernova; contains a pulsar (neutron star) detected as a rapidly pulsating radio and X-ray source [1].

NGC 7293 (Helix Nebula): shell of gas ejected by a Sun-like star at the end of its red giant phase; the central white dwarf is visible as a hot, faint stellar remnant [1].

NGC 4486 (M87): contains a supermassive black hole (~6.5 billion solar masses) evidenced by the orbital speeds of stars and gas near the nucleus, and by jet emission imaged directly with the Event Horizon Telescope [1].

practice_questions.text:
Liam Sutherland, a sixth-form student at the Brackenfell Observing Society in Cumbria, is researching how astronomers have gathered evidence for the existence of black holes without being able to observe them directly.

Describe three distinct lines of observational evidence for black holes. For each piece of evidence, explain the observations made, the physical mechanism linking the observation to a black hole, and what alternative explanations were ruled out.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5-6): Three distinct pieces of evidence each with observation + mechanism + ruling out alternatives. For example:
1. X-ray binaries: X-ray emission from accretion discs in binary systems; gas from companion heated to millions of K spiralling into compact object; companion star orbital period and Doppler shift give mass exceeding 3 solar masses, ruling out white dwarf or neutron star.
2. Stellar orbits near Galactic centre (Sagittarius A*): infrared observations of stars orbiting an invisible point over decades; Kepler's third law gives enclosed mass of ~4 million solar masses in a region small enough to rule out a dense cluster of ordinary stars.
3. Gravitational lensing: light from background galaxies bent into arcs by the gravity of an invisible massive object; mass calculated from arc geometry too large and too compact to be ordinary matter.
Credit also: gravitational wave detections (LIGO mergers), direct imaging by Event Horizon Telescope.

Secure (3-4): Two pieces of evidence with reasonable explanation; one mechanism link clear.

Developing (1-2): One evidence described vaguely; mechanism link absent or wrong.

Emerging (0): Irrelevant or no response.

practice_questions.text:
The Milky Way is classified as which type of galaxy?
A) Elliptical
B) Irregular
C) Barred spiral
D) Lenticular
practice_questions.marks: C [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State two members of the Local Group of galaxies other than the Milky Way, and give the galaxy type of each.
practice_questions.marks:
Any two of (one mark each for correct name + type pair):
• Andromeda Galaxy (M31) — spiral galaxy [1]
• Triangulum Galaxy (M33) — spiral galaxy [1]
• Large Magellanic Cloud (LMC) — irregular galaxy [1]
• Small Magellanic Cloud (SMC) — irregular galaxy [1]

practice_questions.text: Explain why radio astronomers use the 21 cm hydrogen line to map the structure of the Milky Way rather than using an optical telescope.
practice_questions.marks: Optical light is absorbed by dust clouds in the galactic disc, so optical telescopes cannot see through to the far side of the galaxy [1]. Radio waves at 21 cm pass through dust unimpeded [1]. Neutral hydrogen throughout the disc emits at 21 cm, and Doppler shifts in this emission reveal the hydrogen’s velocity, allowing mapping of the spiral arm structure [1].

practice_questions.text: Compare elliptical and spiral galaxies in terms of their star populations, ongoing star formation, and appearance through a telescope.
practice_questions.marks:
Elliptical galaxies:
• Contain mostly old, red stars with little gas or dust [1]
• Little or no ongoing star formation [1]
• Appear as smooth, featureless ellipses; no spiral arms or dust lanes visible [1]

Spiral galaxies:
• Contain both old stars in the bulge and young blue stars in the spiral arms [1]
• Active star formation in the spiral arms where gas and dust are plentiful [1]
• Show spiral arm structure and dust lanes through a telescope; nucleus is a bright point [1]

Mark up to 4: 1 per correct comparison point (max 2 per type).

practice_questions.text: The Andromeda Galaxy (M31) has an apparent magnitude of +3.44 and an absolute magnitude of -21.5. Calculate its distance in parsecs using the distance modulus formula. Show all working.
practice_questions.marks:
Formula: m - M = 5 log10(d) - 5 [1]
Substitution: 3.44 - (-21.5) = 5 log10(d) - 5 → 24.94 = 5 log10(d) - 5 [1]
Rearrangement: log10(d) = (24.94 + 5) / 5 = 29.94 / 5 = 5.988 [1]
Answer: d = 10^5.988 ≈ 970,000 parsecs (accept 10^6 = 1,000,000 pc for M = -21.5 rounded) [1]
(Note: actual distance to M31 is ~770 kpc; accept any answer consistent with correct working from the given magnitudes.)

practice_questions.text:
Niamh O'Sullivan, an astronomer at a university in Dublin, is presenting to the Caerwyn Observatory astronomy club in Wales on the topic of quasars and what they tell us about the history of the universe.

Evaluate the evidence from quasars that supports the Big Bang model of the universe, including: what quasars are and how they produce their luminosity, why their high redshifts are significant, and what the distribution of quasars across cosmic time implies about the early universe.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5-6): Quasars are the most luminous AGN, powered by supermassive black hole accretion discs; explains why the accretion disc (not the black hole itself) is the source; most quasars have very high redshifts placing them at enormous distances and therefore very early in cosmic history (looking back in time); the high number density of quasars at high redshift shows the early universe had more active galactic nuclei, implying the universe has changed over time; this directly contradicts the Steady State model (which predicts the universe looks the same at all epochs) and supports the Big Bang; fewer quasars in the nearby (recent) universe means they faded as black holes ran out of fuel and the universe aged.

Secure (3-4): Correctly describes quasars as luminous AGN; explains high redshift = great distance = early universe; states quasar distribution supports Big Bang over Steady State but may not explain the mechanism fully.

Developing (1-2): Some correct identification of quasars; limited link to Big Bang evidence.

Emerging (0): Irrelevant or no response.

practice_questions.text:
A spectral line with a rest wavelength of 400 nm is observed at 410 nm in a distant galaxy. Which one of the following is the recession velocity of the galaxy?
(Speed of light = 3 × 10^5 km/s)
A) 7,500 km/s
B) 75,000 km/s
C) 750 km/s
D) 750,000 km/s
State what is meant by the cosmic microwave background radiation and give its approximate temperature.
practice_questions.marks: The cosmic microwave background (CMB) is thermal radiation that fills the entire universe uniformly, detected at microwave wavelengths [1]. It has a temperature of approximately 2.7 K [1].

practice_questions.text: A galaxy is observed to have a recession velocity of 4,200 km/s. Using Hubble's law with H0 = 70 km/s/Mpc, calculate its distance in Mpc. Show your working.
Explain how observations of galactic rotation curves provide evidence for the existence of dark matter.
practice_questions.marks: Stars at the outer edges of galaxies are observed to orbit at roughly constant speed regardless of distance from the centre [1]. If only visible matter contributed to gravity, orbital speed should decrease with distance (analogous to outer planets in the Solar System) [1]. The constant rotation speed implies a large amount of unseen mass (dark matter) distributed throughout the galactic halo, providing extra gravitational pull at large distances [1].

practice_questions.text: Compare the Big Bang theory and the Steady State theory as models of the universe. In your answer, state what each model predicts and give two pieces of observational evidence that support the Big Bang and contradict the Steady State.
practice_questions.marks:
Big Bang: universe began in an extremely hot, dense state ~13.8 Gyr ago and has been expanding and cooling since [1]. Steady State: universe has always existed; matter is continuously created to maintain constant average density as the universe expands [1].

Evidence for Big Bang / against Steady State:
• CMB: a uniform 2.7 K radiation field permeates the universe, consistent with cooling from a hot Big Bang; Steady State cannot account for this relic radiation [1]
• Quasar distribution: quasars exist predominantly at high redshifts (early universe), showing the universe was different in the past; Steady State requires the universe to look the same at all epochs [1]
(Also credit: galaxy redshifts implying a finite-age expanding universe.)

practice_questions.text:
Celia Ngozi, a postgraduate student at the Caerwyn Observatory in Wales, is giving a public lecture on the fate of the universe. She presents three possible end scenarios: the Big Freeze, the Big Crunch, and the Big Rip.

For each scenario, describe the physical mechanism and current observational constraints. Evaluate which scenario is best supported by current evidence, and explain the role of dark energy and dark matter in determining the ultimate fate of the universe.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5-6): Describes all three scenarios correctly (Big Freeze: indefinite expansion, stars die, universe cools; Big Crunch: gravity overcomes expansion, universe collapses; Big Rip: dark energy strengthens, tears apart all structure); links each to gravitational vs dark energy balance; correctly identifies Big Freeze as the scenario most consistent with current data (Type Ia supernovae show accelerating expansion driven by constant dark energy); notes dark matter contributes gravitational attraction but is outweighed by dark energy in current models; dark energy is poorly understood and its behaviour in the far future is unknown, making the Big Rip a genuine possibility if dark energy density increases over time; acknowledges uncertainty.

Secure (3-4): Describes all three scenarios, identifies Big Freeze as currently favoured, mentions role of dark energy; some evaluation of uncertainty.

Developing (1-2): Describes one or two scenarios; limited evaluation; dark matter/dark energy confused or absent.

Emerging (0): Irrelevant or no response.
